# Personal Statement

During my three years working at the Community Development Corporation in Boston, I learned that policy work require deep understanding of the communities you serve. My supervisor Maria asked me to help design a new affordable housing initiative, which meant I spent six weeks conducting interviews with forty-two residents in the Roxbury neighborhood to understand their needs and concerns about displacement. I also worked on the CDC's advocacy around zoning reform, attending city council meetings and helping to draft testimony that supported mixed-income development. The experience of hearing directly from residents—like Mrs. Chen, who had lived in her apartment for twenty-three years and was terrified of being priced out, or the Martinez family who needed three bedrooms but could only afford studios—these stories convinced me that data alone cannot drive good policy. Additionally, I served as an AmeriCorps VISTA member for one year before joining the CDC full-time, where I helped coordinate a job training program that placed thirty-one individuals into entry-level positions at local nonprofits and small businesses. This work showed me both the potential and the limitations of local initiatives; we was able to change individual lives but struggled against larger structural barriers in the labor market. I want to pursue a graduate degree in public policy because I believe the field need people who understands both quantitative analysis and the human dimensions of policy problems.

Throughout all of these experiences, I have become increasingly interested in how federal housing policy affects local implementation, particularly in cities like Boston where the cost of living have risen dramatically in the past decade. My work at the CDC have given me concrete understanding of the gap between policy intent and on-the-ground reality. I'm drawn to the connections between housing, economic opportunity, and racial equity—issues that my work in Roxbury have made urgent and personal to me. Going forward, I want to develop skills in policy analysis and research methods so that I can help shape housing initiatives at a regional or state level. A graduate education in public policy will prepared me to move from implementing others' visions to developing my own evidence-based approach to these problems, grounded in the community perspectives I have learned to value.

feedback1:
This is a strong first draft with genuinely compelling material—the specificity you've chosen (Mrs. Chen's twenty-three years, the Martinez family's studio-versus-three-bedroom mismatch, the forty-two interviews, the thirty-one job placements) is exactly the kind of concrete, earned detail that makes an admissions committee trust your commitment to this field. That foundation is solid, so the revision work ahead is about sharpening structure and argument, not rebuilding from scratch.

The most important thing to fix is that the essay doesn't yet make the case for *why this program*. Right now it ends on generic goals—developing "skills in policy analysis and research methods" to work on housing "at a regional or state level"—that could be pasted into an application to almost any public policy program unchanged. Given how specific and vivid your evidence is, you're well-positioned to name a sharper research question (something about the zoning mechanisms you saw in action, or the structural labor-market barriers you gestured at with AmeriCorps but never unpacked) and to connect that question to particular faculty, coursework, or research centers at the program you're applying to. That labor-market observation especially is worth developing—it's one of the more intellectually interesting moments in the piece, and dropping it after one sentence wastes an opportunity to show systems-level thinking.

Related to this, the overall arc needs tightening. Your thesis—that policy work requires both data and human understanding—doesn't surface until the end of a long paragraph of narrative, so readers have to wait to learn why the details matter. Consider signaling that governing idea earlier. Right now the two paragraphs also tend to restate the same insight (the gap between policy intent and on-the-ground reality) rather than each advancing the argument a step further; think of the structure as experience → insight → sharper question → why this program, with each paragraph doing distinct work. Within paragraph one, reordering the AmeriCorps VISTA year chronologically (it happened before the CDC role, but is introduced afterward with "Additionally") will also help the reader follow your trajectory without having to mentally resort the timeline.

At the sentence level, there's a cluster of subject-verb agreement errors worth a careful proofreading pass: "policy work require," "we was able," "the field need people who understands," "the cost of living have risen," "my work... have given," "have made," and "will prepared." None of these are hard fixes, but because your diction is otherwise precise and professional, they stand out and slightly undercut the polished register you've earned elsewhere. While you're proofreading, also look at word repetition—"helped" appears three times in describing three different roles, which flattens your actual level of responsibility (running 42 interviews is more than "helping"), and "understand/understanding" recurs often enough that swapping in synonyms like "insight into" or "grasp of" would add variety. The sentence about Mrs. Chen and the Martinez family is also worth revisiting—the em-dash aside interrupts the main clause enough that the sentence loses its grammatical footing; either drop "these stories" and let "the experience... convinced me" stand as the main clause, or restructure as "Hearing directly from residents... convinced me that..."

Finally, a smaller stylistic note: nearly every sentence in the piece is long and compound, built the same way (subject + elaboration + elaboration). Once you've addressed the structural and fit issues above, consider adding one or two short, direct sentences per paragraph to break up the rhythm—it will help your strongest details land with more punch. But this is polish to apply last; the fit-and-argument work and the grammar cleanup should come first.

# Personal Statement

Policy work requires both rigorous data and a genuine grasp of the communities that data describes; my three years at the Community Development Corporation (CDC) in Boston, following a year as an AmeriCorps VISTA member, taught me that lesson from the ground up. As a VISTA, I coordinated a job training program that placed thirty-one individuals into entry-level positions at local nonprofits and small businesses. The work was rewarding, but it also exposed its own limits: we could change individual lives, yet we kept running into the same structural walls—employers unwilling to offer full-time hours, transportation gaps between where people lived and where jobs actually were, licensing requirements that priced out otherwise qualified candidates. Those barriers stayed with me. When I joined the CDC full-time, my supervisor Maria asked me to design a new affordable housing initiative, and I spent six weeks conducting interviews with forty-two residents in the Roxbury neighborhood to learn about their needs and concerns about displacement. I also worked on the CDC's advocacy around zoning reform, attending city council meetings and drafting testimony that supported mixed-income development. Hearing directly from residents—like Mrs. Chen, who had lived in her apartment for twenty-three years and was terrified of being priced out, or the Martinez family, who needed three bedrooms but could only afford studios—convinced me that data alone cannot drive good policy. It needs a human face.

Throughout these experiences, I became increasingly interested in how federal housing policy affects local implementation, particularly in cities like Boston, where the cost of living has risen dramatically over the past decade. My work at the CDC has given me a concrete grasp of the gap between policy intent and on-the-ground reality, and my time as a VISTA showed me that the same gap exists in labor policy: job training programs can move people into work, but they cannot by themselves fix zoning rules that push people out of the neighborhoods where those jobs exist, or labor markets that offer only unstable, low-wage positions. The two problems are really one problem. That overlap—between where people can afford to live and where they can find dependable work—is the question I want to study in graduate school. I'm drawn to the connections between housing, economic opportunity, and racial equity, issues that my work in Roxbury has made urgent and personal. I want to work with faculty who study regional housing markets and labor economics, take coursework in quantitative policy methods, and draw on research centers focused on housing and economic mobility to examine how zoning reform and workforce development might be designed together, rather than as separate policy silos. A graduate education in public policy will prepare me to move from implementing others' visions to developing my own evidence-based approach to these problems, grounded in the community perspectives I have learned to value.

# Feedback on Your Personal Statement

This is a strong personal statement with excellent material—your specific experiences are concrete and compelling, and your underlying narrative about learning to value community input alongside data is genuinely compelling for a policy school. However, there are several issues preventing this from being as effective as it could be, and I'd like to help you address them.

Let me start with the most significant problem: grammar and agreement errors that, while individually small, accumulate and distract from your message. You have several subject-verb disagreements that need correction. In the first paragraph, you write "policy work require" when it should be "requires"; later you write "the field need people who understands" when it should be "the field needs people who understand." In the second paragraph, "the cost of living have risen" should be "has risen," and "My work at the CDC have given" should be "has given." These errors are particularly noticeable because they occur in sentences where you're making important points, and they undermine your credibility as someone ready for graduate-level work. I'd recommend reading your statement aloud slowly or having someone else read it to catch these, since they're easy to miss when you're close to the text.

There's also one pronoun shift issue: "we was able to change individual lives" should be "we were able to change." These aren't optional corrections—they're grammatical rules, and admissions committees notice them.

Beyond mechanics, I'd encourage you to look at some word choice issues. You write "I served as an AmeriCorps VISTA member for one year before joining the CDC full-time," but this phrasing makes it unclear whether the CDC role was also part-time or full-time. The sentence structure suggests you did AmeriCorps, then joined CDC full-time, which is probably what you mean, but consider clarifying this slightly: "I served as an AmeriCorps VISTA member for one year, then joined the CDC full-time."

More importantly, I notice you use some vague language when describing your motivation. You say you want to pursue a graduate degree because you "believe the field need people"—but admissions committees want to know why *you* specifically are the right person for this program, not just that the field needs certain kinds of people. A small reframe here would strengthen your argument considerably.

Now let me address structure and organization. Your statement does stay on topic and does a good job building a narrative arc from specific experiences to broader ambitions. However, the second paragraph feels somewhat disconnected from the first. You start by describing housing work, then pivot to job training, then back to housing policy. While these are thematically related, the transitions could be smoother. More importantly, the second paragraph repeats some of your core insight from the first—that on-the-ground reality differs from policy intent—without advancing your argument as much as it could. Consider whether you need both the housing and job training details, or whether focusing more deeply on one would be more powerful.

The final sentences also deserve attention. "A graduate education in public policy will prepared me" is grammatically incorrect (should be "will prepare"), but beyond that, this conclusion feels somewhat generic. Many applicants could write something similar. What's specific to you? What do you want to do with this degree that only you, with your particular combination of experience and perspective, would pursue?

Here's what I'd encourage you to do in revision: First, systematically fix all the grammar errors I've identified. Second, strengthen your conclusion by being more specific about what you want to accomplish and how your particular experiences position you uniquely for this work. Third, consider tightening the second paragraph so it advances your narrative rather than simply restating themes from the first. The raw material here is strong—Mrs. Chen's story, the Martinez family's housing needs, the concrete placement numbers—so trust your examples and trim where you're being repetitive. Finally, reconsider the transition between your job training experience and housing policy work; make it clearer why both experiences matter to your trajectory.

You're telling a good story about learning to integrate data with human dimensions of policy. Make sure the writing itself is flawless so that story can shine through.

# Personal Statement

I am applying to pursue a graduate degree in public policy because I want to become someone who can pair rigorous quantitative analysis with a grounded, empathetic understanding of how policy affects the people it is meant to serve. This conviction comes directly from four years of community work in Boston: one year as an AmeriCorps VISTA member, followed by three years at a Community Development Corporation (CDC), where I saw both what local initiatives can accomplish and where they run up against forces no single organization can solve alone.

Before joining the CDC full-time, I spent a year as an AmeriCorps VISTA member coordinating a job training program that placed thirty-one individuals into entry-level positions at local nonprofits and small businesses. The program taught me how much a well-designed local intervention can change an individual life — and how quickly that same intervention runs into structural barriers in the labor market that no single training program could overcome. That tension between individual impact and structural constraint has stayed with me ever since.

It deepened after I joined the CDC full-time. My supervisor, Maria, asked me to help design a new affordable housing initiative, and over six weeks I conducted interviews with forty-two residents in the Roxbury neighborhood to understand their needs and fears about displacement. I heard from residents like Mrs. Chen, who had lived in her apartment for twenty-three years and was terrified of being priced out, and from the Martinez family, who needed three bedrooms but could only afford studios. Their accounts convinced me that data alone cannot drive good policy; it has to be read alongside the lived experience of the people it describes. I carried that conviction into the CDC's advocacy around zoning reform, where I drafted testimony and attended city council meetings in support of mixed-income development. Together, these two roles — one grounded in listening, the other in shaping policy language — showed me that policy work requires not just careful design but a genuine grasp of the community it is meant to serve.

Throughout these experiences, I have grown increasingly interested in how federal housing policy affects local implementation, particularly in cities like Boston, where the cost of living has risen dramatically over the past decade. My time at the CDC has given me a concrete grasp of the gap between policy intent and on-the-ground reality — a gap I saw firsthand in Mrs. Chen's fear of displacement and the Martinez family's housing mismatch. These experiences have made two connections urgent and personal to me: the link between housing stability and economic opportunity, and the role that housing policy plays in narrowing or perpetuating racial inequity in cities like Boston.

A graduate program in public policy would let me build the quantitative and analytical skills I currently lack: rigorous training in econometrics, program evaluation, and housing policy analysis that would let me test, at scale, the patterns I have so far only been able to observe anecdotally. I am particularly drawn to programs with strong methodological training in causal inference and faculty who study regional housing markets and the effects of federal policy on local implementation, since that is precisely the gap I want to help close. My goal is to move from implementing others' visions to designing my own evidence-based housing initiatives at the regional or state level, where I could shape policy on a larger scale than any single CDC. I would also bring something to a cohort built mostly around quantitative training: four years of direct, on-the-ground relationships with residents affected by these policies, and a practiced ability to translate their concerns into concrete language for policymakers. My time in Roxbury has taught me that community trust, once earned, is itself a kind of data — and I want to bring that perspective into a program otherwise focused on models and metrics.

The first thing to address is grammar, specifically subject-verb agreement, because errors of this kind appear so frequently that they will distract any admissions reader from your content. You write "policy work require," "the field need people who understands," "we was able," "cost of living have risen," "my work at the CDC have given," "my work in Roxbury have made," and "will prepared me." Each of these needs correction (requires, needs, understand, were, has risen, has given, has made, will prepare). Because this pattern repeats so often, I'd encourage you to read the essay aloud slowly, sentence by sentence, checking each verb against its subject. This is a mechanical issue but a serious one in a graduate application, since polish signals the same rigor and attention to detail that admissions committees want to see in your future scholarly work.

Beyond grammar, the biggest structural problem is that your first paragraph is trying to do too much. You move from the affordable housing initiative, to the resident interviews, to zoning reform testimony, to the Mrs. Chen and Martinez anecdotes, to your AmeriCorps year, to the job training program, to your reason for pursuing a graduate degree—all in one paragraph. This makes the paragraph read more like a condensed resume than a reflective narrative. Consider breaking this into two or three paragraphs, each organized around a single experience or theme, with room to slow down and reflect on what you learned rather than simply listing what you did. Right now the statement tells us many things you accomplished but doesn't always show us how those experiences changed your thinking or shaped the specific policy questions you want to pursue in graduate school.

This sentence loses its grammatical footing: it opens with "the experience" as the subject but then pivots to "these stories" as if that were the subject, creating a kind of comma splice that muddies an otherwise powerful moment. This is your most vivid material—the human details about Mrs. Chen and the Martinez family—so it deserves a cleaner, more deliberate sentence structure that lets those details land with full force rather than getting tangled in a grammatically confused clause.

In terms of word choice, some of your transitions are functional but flat: "Additionally," "Throughout all of these experiences." These aren't wrong, but they read as placeholders rather than as connective tissue that builds an argument. Since the whole point of a personal statement is to construct a narrative arc—not just a chronological account—your transitions should do more work to show causality and development: how did the AmeriCorps year lead into the CDC work, and how did that work specifically generate the intellectual questions you now want to pursue?

"During my three years working at the Community Development Corporation in Boston, I learned that policy work require deep understanding of the communities you serve" is a serviceable topic sentence, but it's also a fairly generic way to begin a personal statement. Many successful essays open with a specific moment, image, or line of dialogue that draws the reader in before zooming out to context. You already have strong material for this—the image of Mrs. Chen fearing displacement after twenty-three years, for instance, could work beautifully as an opening scene rather than being buried in the middle of a long sentence.

To summarize priorities: fix the subject-verb agreement errors throughout, since they appear repeatedly and undermine the essay's polish; restructure the first paragraph into smaller units organized around distinct experiences with room for reflection; repair the tangled sentence about the resident stories; and most importantly, sharpen the conclusion so that it makes a specific, well-reasoned case for why this graduate program and this next step follow logically from everything you've described. The raw material here is strong—it just needs tighter sentence-level control and a sharper throughline connecting your past experience to your specific future goals.

# Personal Statement

During my three years working at the Community Development Corporation in Boston, I learned that policy work require deep understanding of the communities you serve. My supervisor Maria asked me to help design a new affordable housing initiative, which meant I spent six weeks conducting interviews with forty-two residents in the Roxbury neighborhood to understand their needs and concerns about displacement. I also worked on the CDC's advocacy around zoning reform, attending city council meetings and helping to draft testimony that supported mixed-income development. The experience of hearing directly from residents—like Mrs. Chen, who had lived in her apartment for twenty-three years and was terrified of being priced out, or the Martinez family who needed three bedrooms but could only afford studios—these stories convinced me that data alone cannot drive good policy. Additionally, I served as an AmeriCorps VISTA member for one year before joining the CDC full-time, where I helped coordinate a job training program that placed thirty-one individuals into entry-level positions at local nonprofits and small businesses. This work showed me both the potential and the limitations of local initiatives; we was able to change individual lives but struggled against larger structural barriers in the labor market. I want to pursue a graduate degree in public policy because I believe the field need people who understands both quantitative analysis and the human dimensions of policy problems.

Throughout all of these experiences, I have become increasingly interested in how federal housing policy affects local implementation, particularly in cities like Boston where the cost of living have risen dramatically in the past decade. My work at the CDC have given me concrete understanding of the gap between policy intent and on-the-ground reality. I'm drawn to the connections between housing, economic opportunity, and racial equity—issues that my work in Roxbury have made urgent and personal to me. Going forward, I want to develop skills in policy analysis and research methods so that I can help shape housing initiatives at a regional or state level. A graduate education in public policy will prepared me to move from implementing others' visions to developing my own evidence-based approach to these problems, grounded in the community perspectives I have learned to value.

# Feedback on Your Personal Statement

Overall, your personal statement demonstrates genuine passion for policy work grounded in real experience, and that authenticity is your greatest strength. The specific details—Mrs. Chen's twenty-three years in her apartment, the Martinez family's bedroom needs, the forty-two residents interviewed—make your narrative compelling and credible. Your underlying argument, that good policy requires both data and human understanding, is thoughtful and well-supported by your examples. With some targeted revisions, this can be a strong submission.

Let me start with grammar and mechanics, since these issues distract from your message. You have several subject-verb agreement errors that need correction. In the first paragraph, "policy work require" should be "policy work requires." Later, you write "we was able to change" when it should be "we were able to change." In the second paragraph, "the field need people who understands" should be "the field needs people who understand," and "the cost of living have risen" should be "the cost of living has risen." Finally, "A graduate education in public policy will prepared me" should be "will prepare me." These errors are particularly noticeable in a graduate application because they suggest you haven't carefully proofread your work. I'd recommend reading your statement aloud slowly and checking verb conjugation carefully in a second pass.

Beyond grammar, there are some word choice issues worth addressing. You use "have given me" and "have made" repeatedly in the second paragraph, which creates a slightly awkward rhythm. More importantly, in the first paragraph you write "This work showed me both the potential and the limitations of local initiatives," but "local initiatives" is a bit vague—do you mean job training programs specifically, or community development work more broadly? Being more precise here would strengthen your analysis.

Now, regarding structure and argument: your personal statement follows a logical progression, moving from specific experiences to broader professional goals, and that's good. However, I notice that your two paragraphs address somewhat different questions. The first paragraph answers "Why do you care about policy work?" while the second answers "What kind of policy work interests you specifically, and why do you need graduate school?" These are both important, but the transition between them could be smoother. Right now, the shift from your AmeriCorps and CDC experience to housing policy feels slightly abrupt. You might strengthen this by explicitly connecting your job training experience to housing and economic opportunity earlier, or by restructuring your examples so that housing concerns thread through both paragraphs more consistently.

I also want to gently push back on one aspect of your narrative. You mention that your job training program "placed thirty-one individuals into entry-level positions," but then say you "struggled against larger structural barriers in the labor market." This is realistic and important, but your statement doesn't quite explain what those barriers were or what you learned specifically from that struggle. The connection between "we couldn't solve everything" and "therefore I need graduate school in public policy" could be made more explicit. What structural barriers did you encounter? Why do you think graduate training will help you address them? This specificity would make your case more persuasive.

Finally, consider your closing sentence: "A graduate education in public policy will prepared me to move from implementing others' visions to developing my own evidence-based approach to these problems, grounded in the community perspectives I have learned to value." This is a strong sentiment, but it's slightly generic—many applicants might write something similar. You might strengthen it by being more specific about what evidence-based approach you envision, or what community perspective has most shaped your thinking. This doesn't need to be elaborate, but it could be more distinctive.

One last thought: your statement successfully conveys that you understand policy is about people, not just numbers. That's a valuable insight. Make sure that message comes through clearly by catching those grammar errors and tightening your transitions. Best of luck with your application.

feedback2:
Thank you for sharing this draft. You have real, substantive material here—specific numbers, named individuals, concrete programs—which is exactly what personal statements need to feel credible rather than abstract. The core problem is less about what you're saying and more about polishing the mechanics and sharpening the structure so that the strength of your experience comes through clearly. Let me walk through the issues in order of importance.

The most pressing matter is subject-verb agreement, which appears repeatedly throughout the piece: "policy work require," "the field need people who understands," "we was able to change," "the cost of living have risen," "my work at the CDC have given," "my work in Roxbury have made," and "will prepared me" instead of "will prepare me." These aren't stylistic quibbles—admissions committees read personal statements as evidence of your writing ability, and this many agreement errors in a short piece will distract readers from your content and raise doubts about your attention to detail. I'd recommend reading the essay aloud slowly, sentence by sentence, checking each verb against its subject. This is the single highest-priority fix before anything else.

Next, look at sentence construction, particularly the long sentence about Mrs. Chen and the Martinez family. You set up a list with em dashes ("The experience of hearing directly from residents—like Mrs. Chen... or the Martinez family...") but then the sentence restates its subject awkwardly with "these stories convinced me," which creates a stumbling, run-on effect. Consider breaking this into two sentences: one that introduces the residents and their situations, and a second, cleaner sentence that states the insight you drew from them. Clarity here matters because this is one of the most vivid, human moments in your essay, and you want the sentence structure to support that vividness rather than undercut it.

On structure: the essay currently reads as two large paragraphs, each cramming multiple ideas together, which makes it feel dense and list-like rather than reflective. The first paragraph moves through the housing initiative, the zoning advocacy work, the resident interviews, and then circles back to the AmeriCorps VISTA position—which chronologically came before the CDC job, not after. Reordering this chronologically (VISTA first, then CDC) would help the reader follow your professional trajectory naturally. I'd also suggest breaking this single paragraph into two or three shorter ones, each organized around a distinct experience or insight, so each idea has room to breathe and so the reader isn't asked to hold four different threads in mind at once.

Related to this, the essay leans heavily toward listing accomplishments (forty-two residents, thirty-one placements, six weeks of interviews) without always pausing to explain what you learned or how it changed your thinking. The specificity is good and should stay, but consider pairing each fact with a beat of reflection—not just "this happened" but "this is what it taught me about policy" or "this is the question it left me with." Right now the Mrs. Chen and Martinez examples do this well; the zoning reform and job training sentences could use a similar move.

The transition "Additionally" between the CDC narrative and the VISTA experience feels like a list connector rather than a narrative bridge. Personal statements benefit from transitions that show causal or thematic connection—for instance, explaining how the VISTA experience shaped your approach to the later CDC role, or how the limitations you saw in the job training program directly fed your interest in graduate study. Right now the paragraph reads as chronological accumulation rather than a building argument.

The second paragraph is where the essay's purpose—persuading an admissions committee that graduate school is the right next step for you—needs the most development, and right now it's the essay's weakest section. It restates themes from paragraph one (the gap between policy and reality, the importance of community perspective) without adding much new. What's missing is specificity about the graduate program itself: what particular skills, coursework, methods, or even faculty/research areas draw you to this degree, and ideally to this particular school or program. "I want to pursue a graduate degree in public policy" is generic; admissions committees want to see that you've thought concretely about what a graduate education will give you that your work experience hasn't, and why this program in particular is suited to that. Right now you gesture at "policy analysis and research methods" but don't specify which methods, which policy areas, or which career outcome you're aiming for beyond "regional or state level" work. Naming a specific interest—say, housing finance policy, quantitative program evaluation, or a particular federal-local policy tension you want to study—would make your goals feel concrete rather than aspirational in the abstract.

Finally, consider your opening. Starting with "During my three years working at the Community Development Corporation in Boston, I learned that..." is a competent but fairly conventional opening move for a personal statement. Since you already have vivid material in Mrs. Chen's story, you might consider opening with a brief scene or moment from that interview process, then zooming out to the three years of experience. This would immediately establish voice and stakes rather than easing in with a summary sentence.

To prioritize: fix the grammar errors first, since they're numerous and undermine credibility regardless of content quality. Then work on paragraph structure, breaking the two dense paragraphs into more focused units organized chronologically and thematically. Then strengthen the second half by adding specific, concrete detail about what you want from graduate study and why, since right now it's the section furthest from fulfilling the statement's actual purpose of persuading an admissions committee that you belong in their specific program.

# Personal Statement

Mrs. Chen sat across from me at her kitchen table, work-worn hands wrapped around a cup of tea, and told me she had lived in the same Roxbury apartment for twenty-three years. She was terrified of being priced out. Her fear stayed with me long after that interview ended, and it became one of the central reasons I decided to pursue a graduate degree in public policy. During my three years working at the Community Development Corporation (CDC) in Boston, and in the year I spent beforehand as an AmeriCorps VISTA member, I learned that policy work requires a deep understanding of the communities it is meant to serve.

Before joining the CDC full-time, I served for one year as an AmeriCorps VISTA member, where I helped coordinate a job training program that placed thirty-one individuals into entry-level positions at local nonprofits and small businesses. Watching these placements succeed taught me that local initiatives can change individual lives in tangible, immediate ways. But I also saw the limits of that impact: many participants who found jobs still struggled with wages that failed to keep pace with rising housing costs, and I began to recognize that no amount of local coordination could resolve structural barriers embedded in the broader labor market. That tension—between what local programs can achieve and what they cannot—is what first pushed me to think about policy at a larger scale.

That question followed me into my work at the CDC, where my supervisor, Maria, asked me to help design a new affordable housing initiative. Over six weeks, I conducted interviews with forty-two residents in Roxbury to understand their needs and concerns about displacement. Mrs. Chen was one of them; the Martinez family, who needed three bedrooms but could only afford studios, were another. Their stories convinced me that data alone cannot drive good policy—that numbers on affordability gaps mean little without an understanding of the lives behind them. I also worked on the CDC's advocacy around zoning reform, attending city council meetings and helping draft testimony that supported mixed-income development. That experience showed me how slowly policy change moves even when the human need is urgent, and it sharpened my interest in understanding the mechanisms—zoning law, subsidy structures, local political incentives—that determine whether good intentions translate into built housing.

Throughout these experiences, I have become increasingly interested in how federal housing policy affects local implementation, particularly in cities like Boston, where the cost of living has risen dramatically over the past decade. My work at the CDC has given me a concrete understanding of the gap between policy intent and on-the-ground reality, and my time in Roxbury has made the connections between housing, economic opportunity, and racial equity feel urgent and personal rather than abstract. What I lack, and what I am seeking in graduate study, are the analytical tools to address these problems at scale: training in quantitative program evaluation, housing finance policy, and the methods used to assess how federal subsidy structures interact with local zoning authority. I am particularly interested in coursework and research that examine why affordable housing programs succeed in some municipalities and stall in others, so that I can eventually help shape housing initiatives at a regional or state level. A graduate education in public policy will prepare me to move from implementing others' visions to developing my own evidence-based approach to these problems, grounded in the community perspectives I have learned to value.

# Personal Statement

My interest in molecular biology began when I learned about the structure of DNA in tenth grade, and I found myself fascinated by how the double helix work and how genetic information are passed down through generations. During my undergraduate years at State University, I have taken advanced courses in biochemistry and cell biology, and I was volunteering in Dr. Patricia Chen's lab where I studied protein misfolding in neurodegeneration. This experience were transformative because I got to see how molecular research translates into understanding disease. In Dr. Chen's lab, I worked on analyzing aggregation patterns of tau protein in Alzheimer's models, running Western blots and immunofluorescence assays three times a week for eighteen months. The work was challenging and repetitive but also deeply satisfying—there is something powerful about watching a hypothesis either confirmed or disproven by your own hands. After my junior year, I was selected to present my findings at the Northeast Undergraduate Research Conference, which was a validating moment that make me realize I belong in this field.

Graduate school represents the next logical step for my trajectory, and I am committed to pursuing research that addresses neurodegenerative disease at the molecular level. My experience in Dr. Chen's lab have prepared me with technical skills and also with the patience and precision that molecular biology demands. I am particularly drawn to your program because of Professor James Morrison's recent publications on protein dynamics and his lab's innovative use of cryo-EM technology, which represents exactly the kind of cutting-edge work I wants to contribute to. Moving forward, I hope to develop into an independent researcher who can design experiments and mentors younger students, and I believe your institution provide the resources and mentorship necessary for this goal. Molecular biology have taught me that small discoveries builds understanding, and I am ready to dedicate myself to this field completely.

feedback1:
This is a solid draft with the right structural bones—it moves logically from origin of interest through research experience to future goals and program fit, and it stays entirely on topic throughout. But it currently reads as competent rather than compelling, and the reason is consistent across every level of the writing: the most specific, most *you* content is gestured at rather than shown. The opening DNA anecdote is a common entry point for this kind of essay, and the lab description tells us what assays you ran and how often but not what you actually learned, discovered, or contributed intellectually. Since you clearly had enough of a finding to present at a conference, naming that finding—even briefly—would demonstrate ownership of the science rather than just diligence in the lab. The same thinness shows up in the section on Professor Morrison: right now the fit is asserted through adjectives ("cutting-edge," "innovative") rather than demonstrated through a real connection between what you already know about tau and protein aggregation and the specific open question in his cryo-EM work you'd want to pursue. That paragraph is the natural place to make the strongest, most persuasive case in the whole essay, and currently it's the thinnest part. The closing goals are similarly generic ("independent researcher who can design experiments and mentor students" is the default aspiration in nearly every essay in this genre); tying that ambition explicitly to your specific disease focus and techniques would make the ending feel earned rather than templated. This same pattern—strong technical vocabulary (Western blots, tau protein, cryo-EM) sitting alongside vague evaluative language ("transformative," "validating," "powerful," "small discoveries build understanding")—shows up throughout, and the fix is the same everywhere: replace the abstract, stock phrasing with the same precision you already use when discussing your actual bench work.

Once you've sharpened the content, there are a number of grammatical errors worth cleaning up—mostly subject-verb agreement ("the double helix work" should be "works," "this experience were" should be "was," "your institution provide" should be "provides," and several others), plus one parallelism slip ("design experiments and mentors younger students" should be "mentor"). These are easy fixes and won't take long, but they should be corrected carefully since a personal statement is expected to be polished.

Beyond content and grammar, both paragraphs rely heavily on the same sentence shape—two clauses joined by "and"—which creates a flattening, repetitive rhythm just when the content (escalating lab responsibility, a conference presentation, future ambition) should feel like it's building momentum. Breaking a few of these into shorter standalone sentences or subordinate clauses would let the pacing match the energy of what you're describing. Relatedly, the transition between paragraphs is a little abrupt: paragraph one ends on the emotional high of the conference, and paragraph two opens with "Graduate school represents the next logical step," without quite explaining why that specific experience pointed you toward this next step. A bridging sentence there would smooth the arc.

None of this requires restructuring the essay—the shape and organization are sound. The highest-value revision is deepening the substance in the two places that matter most to an admissions reader: what you actually discovered in Dr. Chen's lab, and why Morrison's specific research question, not just his lab's reputation, is the right next step for the thinking you've already started. Tightening the grammar and varying the sentence rhythm afterward will bring the polish the content deserves.

# Personal Statement

My interest in molecular biology began when I learned about the structure of DNA in tenth grade. I found myself fascinated by how the double helix works and how genetic information is passed down through generations. During my undergraduate years at State University, I took advanced courses in biochemistry and cell biology. I also volunteered in Dr. Patricia Chen's lab, where I studied protein misfolding in neurodegeneration. This experience showed me, for the first time, how molecular research translates into understanding disease. In Dr. Chen's lab, I worked on analyzing aggregation patterns of tau protein in Alzheimer's models, running Western blots and immunofluorescence assays three times a week for eighteen months. Over that time, I found that a particular phosphorylated tau isoform aggregated more rapidly under oxidative stress conditions than its unmodified counterpart—a pattern that suggested phosphorylation state, not just protein concentration, might drive early aggregation kinetics. The work was repetitive, but each blot brought me closer to seeing whether that pattern would hold. After my junior year, I presented this finding at the Northeast Undergraduate Research Conference. Defending my data in front of researchers outside my own lab made me realize that I could hold my own asking and answering questions about tau biology, not just running the protocols someone else had designed.

That shift, from executing an experiment to owning its interpretation, is what convinced me graduate school was the right next step. Graduate school represents the next logical step for my trajectory. I am committed to pursuing research that addresses neurodegenerative disease at the molecular level. My experience in Dr. Chen's lab has prepared me with technical skills; it has also given me the patience and precision that molecular biology demands. I am particularly drawn to your program because of Professor James Morrison's recent work using cryo-EM to resolve structural intermediates in tau fibril formation. My own data pointed to phosphorylation-dependent differences in aggregation kinetics, but Western blot and immunofluorescence could only tell me that aggregation was happening faster, not what the intermediate structures actually looked like. Morrison's approach to capturing those transient conformations is exactly the tool I need to pursue the next question my undergraduate work raised. Moving forward, I hope to develop into an independent researcher who can design experiments probing the structural basis of tau aggregation and mentor younger students through that same process of discovery. I believe your institution provides the resources and mentorship necessary for this goal. My work with Dr. Chen taught me that a single aggregation assay, repeated carefully enough, can reveal a mechanism no one has described before. I am ready to bring that same persistence to resolving the structural questions that remain open in this field.

Additionally, "your institution provide" should be "provides," and "Molecular biology have taught me that small discoveries builds understanding" contains two agreement errors—it should be "has taught" and "build." These mistakes appear frequently enough that a careful proofreading pass is essential.

Beyond grammar, look at your verb tense consistency. You write "During my undergraduate years at State University, I have taken advanced courses," but then shift to past tense with "I was volunteering." Since you're writing about completed experiences, past tense would be more consistent throughout. The phrase "which was a validating moment that make me realize" also contains an awkward construction—consider simplifying to something like "which validated my sense that I belong in this field."

Your word choices are generally strong, but a few phrases could be more precise. You write that you "got to see how molecular research translates into understanding disease," which is somewhat informal for a graduate application. Consider language like "witnessed" or "gained insight into how." Similarly, "there is something powerful about watching a hypothesis either confirmed or disproven by your own hands" is evocative but slightly awkward. The phrase "by your own hands" feels colloquial; "through your own work" would be more polished.

In terms of structure and content, your statement effectively traces a logical progression from initial interest through undergraduate research to future goals. However, the second paragraph tries to accomplish too much. You're introducing your motivation for graduate school, demonstrating knowledge of your target program, discussing future aspirations, and making a broader philosophical statement about molecular biology—all in relatively few sentences. Consider whether every element deserves space or whether some ideas could be condensed or cut entirely. For instance, your statement that you want to "mentor younger students" is fine but doesn't add as much value as deepening your explanation of why Professor Morrison's work specifically excites you.

Speaking of which, you mention that you're "particularly drawn to your program because of Professor James Morrison's recent publications on protein dynamics and his lab's innovative use of cryo-EM technology." This is good—it shows you've done your homework—but you could strengthen it by being more specific about what aspect of his work connects to your own research interests or future goals. How does his work on protein dynamics relate to your tau protein research? Making this connection explicit would show sophisticated thinking about your fit with the program.

The opening of your statement is strong and personal, grounding your interest in a specific moment. However, the closing is less effective. Your final sentence—"Molecular biology have taught me that small discoveries builds understanding, and I am ready to dedicate myself to this field completely"—is somewhat generic and contains the grammatical errors mentioned above. Beyond the grammar, this conclusion doesn't offer a memorable takeaway. Consider ending with something that more specifically articulates what drives you or what you hope to achieve, perhaps tying back to your early fascination with how biological systems work.

Finally, while your statement demonstrates technical knowledge and genuine engagement with research, you might strengthen your narrative by briefly reflecting on what you learned from the challenges you faced. You mention the work was "challenging and repetitive," which is honest, but you don't explain how those challenges shaped you as a researcher or what they taught you about the field. Admissions committees want to see not just what you did, but what you learned from it.

In summary, prioritize fixing the grammatical errors first, then consider tightening the second paragraph to focus on your strongest connections to your target program, and finally, refine your opening and closing to ensure they're polished and specific rather than generic. With these revisions, you'll have a strong statement that shows both your qualifications and your authentic enthusiasm for this work.

A single diagram in my tenth-grade biology textbook—the double helix, unwinding to reveal the code beneath—held my attention long after the class moved on to something else. I wanted to know how something so small could carry information across generations, and that curiosity has shaped every academic decision I have made since.

At State University, I took advanced coursework in biochemistry and cell biology, then volunteered in Dr. Patricia Chen's lab, where I studied protein misfolding in neurodegeneration. For eighteen months, I analyzed aggregation patterns of tau protein in Alzheimer's models, running Western blots and immunofluorescence assays three times a week. I learned to troubleshoot failed antibody stains, to distinguish real aggregation signal from background noise, and to accept that a clean result might take a dozen attempts to produce. Watching a hypothesis confirmed or disproven by my own hands, week after week, taught me more about the discipline research requires than any lecture had.

After my junior year, I was selected to present my findings at the Northeast Undergraduate Research Conference. Standing before researchers who asked pointed questions about my data—about controls I had run, alternative explanations I had considered—I realized that the patience I had built in the lab translated into the ability to defend an idea under scrutiny. That exchange, more than the poster itself, told me I could hold my own in this field.

I want to continue investigating neurodegenerative disease at the molecular level, and graduate training is what will let me move from executing assigned protocols to designing my own experiments and asking my own questions about how misfolded proteins spread and aggregate.

Your program is an especially strong fit because of Professor James Morrison's work on protein dynamics using cryo-EM. My work with tau taught me to characterize aggregation through indirect readouts—antibody binding, fluorescence intensity—but I never had the tools to see the structural intermediates that determine whether a misfolded protein resolves harmlessly or seeds further aggregation. I want to use cryo-EM to visualize those intermediate conformations directly, and to ask how specific structural features of tau oligomers influence their propagation between cells.

Long term, I want to build a research program centered on the structural basis of protein aggregation in neurodegenerative disease, with an eye toward identifying features that could be targeted therapeutically. I also want to mentor undergraduates the way Dr. Chen mentored me—by giving them ownership of a piece of a larger question early enough that they feel the stakes of their own data.

The double helix that caught my attention in tenth grade is not, on its own, what pulls me toward this work anymore. What pulls me now is the misfolded protein under the microscope, resisting a clean story, waiting for someone patient enough to work out how it becomes dangerous—and I want your program to be where I do that work.

In tenth grade biology, our teacher passed around a model of the DNA double helix and posed a question that stuck with me: how could a molecule built from just four repeating units encode the instructions for an entire organism? I did not have an answer then, but the question stayed with me through high school and into college, where it eventually became the foundation of my academic path.

During my undergraduate years at State University, I took advanced courses in biochemistry and cell biology, and I volunteered in Dr. Patricia Chen's lab, where I studied protein misfolding in neurodegeneration. This experience was transformative because I got to see how molecular research translates into understanding disease.

In Dr. Chen's lab, I worked on analyzing aggregation patterns of tau protein in Alzheimer's models, running Western blots and immunofluorescence assays three times a week for eighteen months. The work was challenging and repetitive but also deeply satisfying—there is something powerful about watching a hypothesis either confirmed or disproven by your own hands. One pattern we observed—that aggregation appeared to cluster along specific axonal regions rather than distributing evenly throughout the neuron—raised a question I still think about: whether the location of misfolding is a cause of neuronal dysfunction or merely a downstream marker of it. That open question is part of what draws me toward graduate research rather than away from it. After my junior year, I was selected to present my findings at the Northeast Undergraduate Research Conference, a validating moment that made me realize I belong in this field.

Graduate school represents the next step in my academic path, and I am committed to pursuing research that addresses neurodegenerative disease at the molecular level. My experience in Dr. Chen's lab has prepared me with technical skills, and it has also given me the patience and precision that molecular biology demands.

My work with tau aggregation left me with an unresolved question about the conformational states that misfolded proteins pass through before they form stable aggregates—a question that assays like Western blotting cannot answer on their own. Your first sentence is a comma splice—you've joined two independent clauses with only a comma after "English class." Similarly, the second sentence ("I spent the next two years reading widely, I picked up translations...") has the same problem. These errors accumulate and suggest a lack of careful revision, which matters in an application where precision demonstrates respect for the reader.

Beyond mechanics, I want to address the overall structure of your argument. Both paragraphs are quite long and dense, which makes them harder to follow and dilutes your most important points. The first paragraph is primarily narrative—it shows your intellectual evolution, which is valuable—but it lacks a clear thesis or takeaway. What is the larger insight you've reached? The second paragraph tries to accomplish too much: it explains why you're applying, references specific faculty, mentions your research experience, and articulates your future research questions. These elements are all worth including, but they're tangled together in ways that obscure rather than highlight your thinking.

The vocabulary and phrasing generally serve you well, but there are moments where you could be more precise. In the second paragraph, "seems directly relevant" (note: "seminars" is plural, so this should be "seem") uses imprecise language where you could be more assertive about the connection. If these courses are genuinely central to your interests, say so directly rather than tentatively.

More significantly, I notice you name Gabriel Allende in your thesis description, but I suspect you mean Isabel Allende, author of *The House of the Spirits*. This kind of error in a personal statement is particularly damaging because it's your opportunity to showcase expertise. Double-check all names and titles, and consider whether you can verify these details are correct.

There's real intellectual substance here—your grasp of comparative literature's core questions (form and ideology, translation and meaning, the politics of a "global literary conversation") is sophisticated and genuinely graduate-level. That's the most important thing, and it's working in your favor. But the prose itself needs significant revision before it does justice to that thinking, so let me walk through the issues in order of priority.

The most pressing problem is comma splices, which appear repeatedly and will read as careless to an admissions committee, regardless of how strong your ideas are. "The magical realism in that novel fascinated me and I wanted to understand..." needs a period or semicolon before "the magical realism," not a comma. Similarly, "I spent the next two years reading widely, I picked up translations..." splices two independent clauses. Later, "I am interested in pursuing a PhD and potentially teaching and researching how comparative study illuminates what we think literature can do, I am particularly drawn to questions..." does the same thing, and by this point the sentence has become a long chain of loosely connected ideas that would benefit from being broken into two or three separate sentences. Go through the whole piece hunting for these; they're the single most fixable issue and the one most likely to distract a careful reader from your content.

There's also a factual/naming error you should catch: you refer to "Gabriel Allende," but the author of *The House of the Spirits* is Isabel Allende. This is a significant slip in a statement about literary expertise—exactly the kind of detail an admissions reader in this field will notice, so proofread names with extra care.

On subject-verb agreement and small grammar points: "different cultures approaches storytelling differently" should be "different cultures approach storytelling differently." "Your graduate seminars... and the recent course... seems directly relevant" should be "seem," since the subject is plural (seminars and course).

Structurally, the first paragraph is doing a lot of work—tracing high school, two years of independent reading, a college seminar, and a senior thesis—and it moves chronologically, which is a reasonable spine, but each stage is described in a single dense sentence, so the paragraph feels breathless rather than developed. Consider letting your best example (the thesis comparing Stoker and Allende) have more room to breathe, since it's your strongest and most specific evidence of original scholarly thinking. You could trim the earlier reading list (Murakami, Lispector, Cortázar) to a briefer mention, since right now it's just named rather than analyzed, whereas the thesis section actually shows your analytical method.

The second paragraph tries to do several things at once—state your reasons for applying, gesture at your intellectual commitments, name specific faculty offerings, describe your RA experience, and preview your research interests—and as a result some connections feel underdeveloped. The phrase "also I believe strongly that literature is a way to understand human experience across difference" is vague and reads as an afterthought bolted onto the sentence before it; this kind of broad humanistic claim doesn't add much and could either be cut or be made more specific to your actual research question. Similarly, tie your RA experience more explicitly to your stated interests: you say the lab experience taught you about "granular choices" translators make, which is good, but connect this directly to the questions about meaning and cultural travel you raise just before it, so the paragraph reads as cumulative rather than list-like.

One more structural note: you never explicitly name the specific faculty members or scholars whose work you're drawing on, even though you say you're applying "because of your faculty's work on translation and world literature." If you have specific names, include them—it signals genuine fit and research, rather than a generic gesture toward "translation and world literature" that could apply to many programs.

Finally, consider your closing. Right now the piece ends on a strong intellectual question (whether a "global literary conversation" is itself a Western imposition), which is a great note to end on conceptually, but the statement doesn't circle back to remind the reader of your trajectory or make a final case for fit. A brief closing sentence that ties your past work, your current questions, and this specific program together would give the piece a stronger sense of closure rather than trailing off on a subordinate clause.

In terms of priority: fix the comma splices and the Allende error first, since these are the kinds of errors that undercut credibility fastest. Then work on paragraph pacing—giving your strongest example more space and trimming the more general gestures—and finally, tighten the connections between your evidence (thesis, RA work) and your stated research questions so the whole statement reads as a coherent argument for why you specifically belong in this specific program.

# Personal Statement

My interest in comparative literature began in my junior year of high school when I read Gabriel García Márquez's *One Hundred Years of Solitude* in English class. The magical realism in that novel fascinated me, and I wanted to understand how different cultures approach storytelling differently. Over the next two years, I read widely, picking up translations of works by Haruki Murakami, Clarice Lispector, and Julio Cortázar, and I was struck by the recurring motifs of isolation and cyclical time across these texts written in different languages and contexts. In college, I took a seminar on Latin American narrative where we analyzed how colonialism shaped narrative structure itself, comparing the fragmented timeline of *The House of the Spirits* to the linear, authoritative voice in colonial chronicles; this revelation made me realize that form is never neutral.

This idea became the foundation of my senior thesis, which examined epistolary techniques in nineteenth-century European and South American novels. I focused specifically on how Bram Stoker uses multiple documents to create unreliability, while Isabel Allende uses them to establish feminine authority. Working through these two authors side by side showed me how the same formal strategy can carry entirely different ideological weight depending on the cultural and historical context in which it emerges, and it gave me a method I want to keep using: reading formal choices as historically and politically situated rather than universal.

I am applying to your program because of Professor [Name]'s work on translation theory and Professor [Name]'s scholarship on affect in world literature. I want to continue studying how narratives travel across linguistic and cultural boundaries and what happens to meaning in that process. Your graduate seminars on modernism in multiple traditions and your recent course on affect across world literatures seem directly relevant to my interests. My experience as a research assistant in my university's translation lab, where I worked on translating contemporary Argentine short stories, gave me direct insight into the granular choices translators make and how those choices reshape a text for new readers; that work is what first made the question of "what happens to meaning" concrete for me, rather than abstract. I am interested in pursuing a PhD and, eventually, teaching and researching how comparative study illuminates what we think literature can do. I am particularly drawn to questions about how formal innovation in one tradition influences another, and whether there exists something like a global literary conversation or whether that idea itself is a kind of Western imposition. My past work on form and ideology, my hands-on experience with translation, and your faculty's research on translation and world literature together make me confident that your program is the right place to pursue these questions.

# Feedback on Your Personal Statement

Your personal statement demonstrates genuine intellectual curiosity and a well-developed scholarly trajectory, which are strengths. You've clearly thought about how form and meaning interact across literary traditions, and your concrete examples—the seminar on Latin American narrative, your thesis work on epistolary techniques—show rather than tell. However, the passage needs revision in several key areas to be most effective for graduate applications.

**Grammar and mechanics** are your most pressing concern. The first paragraph contains a comma splice after "English class"—you've joined two independent clauses with only a comma. Later, you have another significant comma splice: "I want to continue studying how narratives travel across linguistic and cultural boundaries, and what happens to that process, also I believe strongly..." The word "also" signals a new independent clause, so a period or semicolon is needed before it. These errors suggest the work hasn't been carefully proofread, which matters for an application where admissions committees assess writing quality. Beyond comma splices, watch for agreement issues: "different cultures approaches storytelling" should be "approach" (plural subject). Similarly, near the end you write "Gabriel Allende" when you likely mean Isabel Allende. These small errors accumulate and distract from your ideas.

More substantively, your **organization and emphasis** need recalibration. Right now, you front-load your intellectual development (high school interest through senior thesis) before explaining why you're applying to this specific program. While the narrative of intellectual growth is valuable, it takes up roughly sixty percent of your statement. For a graduate application, admissions committees want to understand your fit with their program and your research agenda relatively quickly. Consider restructuring: you might briefly establish your intellectual interests in comparative literature, then pivot much earlier to what you're seeking in graduate study and why this program specifically matters to you. Your second paragraph addresses the program, but it's somewhat reactive—you're listing things the program offers and matching them to your interests. Instead, articulate what you want to *do* or *discover* in graduate school, then explain how this program enables that work.

**Specificity is also important here.** You mention interest in the faculty's work on translation and world literature, but you don't name specific faculty members or discuss their research. Graduate applications are stronger when you demonstrate you've done real homework on the program—you know whose work you want to engage with and why. Similarly, you mention "seminars on modernism in multiple traditions" and "the recent course on affect across world literatures," but these remain vague. If you're actually interested in these courses, say why they matter to your research questions.

**Your core research questions**, which appear late in the statement, are actually your strongest material. The questions about whether formal innovation travels between traditions and whether "global literary conversation" is real or a Western imposition are sophisticated and original. These should be more prominent because they're specific enough to show genuine scholarly engagement and ambitious enough to justify graduate study. Right now, they get buried at the end alongside other interests. Highlight your actual research direction earlier and use it as an anchor for why this program fits.

The **vocabulary and tone** are generally strong—you sound like a serious reader who thinks carefully about literature. However, some phrasing could be tightened. The phrase "what happens to meaning in that process, also I believe strongly that literature is a way to understand human experience across difference" mixes a specific analytical interest with a broader humanistic statement that feels less distinctive. The personal conviction about literature's value is fine to include, but it's common enough that it doesn't distinguish your application. Focus instead on what's unusual about your thinking.

You tell us about your intellectual development and your research interests, which is appropriate, but you could strengthen the statement by briefly indicating what kind of scholar you want to become or what motivates this research beyond intellectual interest. Is there a broader scholarly conversation you want to contribute to? A specific gap in the field you want to address? These details would make your application more memorable.

In revision, proofread carefully for the grammatical errors I've noted, reorganize to move your research questions and program-specific interest earlier, and develop more specific engagement with the program's faculty and curriculum.

Sentences like "I spent the next two years reading widely, I picked up translations of works by..." and "the magical realism in that novel fascinated me and I wanted to understand..." string together independent clauses with only a comma or no punctuation at all, which makes the prose feel breathless and unedited. # Personal Statement

I am drawn to comparative literature because of a single question that keeps returning in different forms: how does literary form travel across languages and cultures, and what is transformed—or even invented—in that crossing? This question first found me in my junior year of high school, when I read Gabriel García Márquez's *One Hundred Years of Solitude* in English class. The novel's magical realism captivated me. I wanted to understand how different cultures approach storytelling differently, and why some techniques seemed to cross borders more easily than others.

Over the next two years, I read widely to pursue that question. I picked up translations of works by Haruki Murakami, Clarice Lispector, and Julio Cortázar. Across these texts, written in different languages and contexts, I noticed recurring motifs of isolation and cyclical time. Their persistence across such different traditions suggested to me that literature might participate in something like a shared conversation. Yet I remained unsure whether that conversation was genuinely global, or simply a product of which books happened to get translated and taught.

In college, I took a seminar on Latin American narrative that sharpened this interest into a more rigorous method. We analyzed how colonialism shaped narrative structure itself, comparing the fragmented timeline of *The House of the Spirits* to the linear, authoritative voice of colonial chronicles. This comparison taught me that form is never neutral; it carries the imprint of the power structures in which it was produced.

My senior thesis extended this insight to epistolary technique in nineteenth-century fiction. I compared two novels built from multiple documents: Bram Stoker's *Dracula* and José Mármol's *Amalia*. Stoker assembles letters, diaries, and newspaper clippings to build a sense of unreliability. Mármol, by contrast, uses correspondence to construct political testimony and interior resistance to tyranny. The same formal device—fragmentary, multiple documents—produced opposite effects in each text. That contrast convinced me that formal strategies cannot be studied apart from the historical and ideological contexts in which they take shape.

I am applying to your program because of your faculty's work on translation and world literature, particularly Professor Elena Vasquez's scholarship on affect and cross-cultural narrative form and Professor Daniel Cho's work on translation theory. I want to continue studying how narratives move across linguistic and cultural boundaries, and what happens to meaning in that process. Your graduate seminar on modernism in multiple traditions speaks directly to my interest in formal innovation, and your recent course on affect across world literatures would let me pursue, in a more theoretical register, the questions about emotion and interiority that first drew me to Lispector and Murakami.

I have experience as a research assistant in my university's translation lab, where I worked on translating contemporary Argentine short stories. This work gave me insight into the granular choices translators make and how those choices reshape a text for new readers. It also gave me a practical, sentence-level understanding of the theoretical questions I had only encountered in seminar discussion.

I am interested in pursuing a PhD, and eventually teaching and researching, because I want to keep asking how comparative study illuminates what we think literature can do. I am particularly drawn to questions about how formal innovation in one tradition influences another. I am also convinced that literature offers one of the clearest ways to understand human experience across difference, even as I remain skeptical of any claim that this understanding is automatic or innocent. That skepticism is what animates my central question: whether there exists something like a global literary conversation, or whether that idea is itself a kind of Western imposition.

I do not yet have a settled answer to that question, and I suspect I will not have one for a long time. But I want to spend a PhD, and a career, pursuing it with the same rigor my undergraduate work taught me to bring to a single fragmented sentence or a single translated letter. Your program's attention to both translation and form makes it the place where I believe I can do that work most seriously.

# Feedback on Your Personal Statement

Your personal statement has a solid foundation: you've identified genuine experiences that shaped your interest in mechanical engineering, and you're making an effort to connect those experiences to your graduate aspirations. You mention the solar car project nine times across just two paragraphs, and you repeat the phrase "working on the solar car project" or variations of it at least five times. While repetition can be a useful rhetorical device, here it feels like filler rather than emphasis. Each time you circle back to the same project without introducing new details or insights, you're using valuable space that could develop your narrative more compellingly. I'd recommend keeping only the most significant details about each experience and trusting that you've made your point after mentioning something once or twice.

Related to this is an **issue with specificity and depth**. Rather than telling us repeatedly that you worked on the solar car, show us *why* that work mattered to you. You mention learning CAD and understanding weight-reduction tradeoffs, but you don't explain what specifically you discovered or how these insights shaped your thinking. For instance, what was a particular design challenge you faced? Did you fail at something important? How did that failure inform your approach to engineering? The Anderson Manufacturing section does slightly better here—the twelve percent cycle time reduction is concrete—but even that could be more vivid if you explained what problem you solved and why it matters. Graduate admissions committees want to understand not just what you did, but how you think and what you learned.

Your **sentence structure and vocabulary** also need attention. Many of your sentences are straightforward but somewhat plain: "I worked on the suspension system and I worked on optimizing the aerodynamics" repeats the subject and verb unnecessarily. More problematically, your word choices are quite general. You use phrases like "learned a lot," "made me realize," and "showed me" repeatedly, which are safe but forgettable. Consider using more precise language: instead of "learned about mechanical engineering in the real world," you might say something that captures what aspect of the discipline genuinely intrigued you. What specifically about solving those problems felt different from coursework?

While it's appropriate to be professional, a personal statement should sound like *you*—someone with genuine enthusiasm and a particular way of seeing the world.
