# Personal Statement

The suspension arm didn't fit. I had modeled it in CAD for weeks, accounting for load distribution and material stress, but when I mounted it on the frame, the geometry conflicted with a structural element I hadn't accounted for. That moment was my real introduction to mechanical engineering: not equations on a page, but the gap between a model and a physical object.

That gap became familiar to me while working on my university's solar car project, a team-based initiative in which students design and build a solar-powered vehicle to compete in a cross-country race. I was responsible for the suspension system, where most of my time was spent negotiating the tradeoff between weight reduction and structural integrity. Reducing weight meant thinner components and fewer redundancies. Too much reduction risked failure under the stresses of the race route. I learned to iterate: model, simulate, test, revise. Some solutions came from software; others came from conversations with teammates who understood loads and materials better than I did. Meeting weekly with a team of five other students to review our designs taught me that mechanical engineering depends as much on communication as on calculation.

By the end of the project, I understood tradeoffs like this in a way coursework alone couldn't have taught me. More importantly, I found the kind of problem I want to keep solving: one where competing constraints must be balanced under real limitations. That is the work I want to pursue in graduate study, particularly in design optimization, where I hope to develop more rigorous tools for approaching exactly these tradeoffs.

I carried that same instinct into two summers as an intern at Anderson Manufacturing, working on injection molding processes and tooling design. During that time, I noticed that one mold sat idle far longer than the others during changeovers, and cycle-time data suggested the issue was in how the tooling was configured for a specific part geometry. After learning lean manufacturing principles through manuals and training sessions, I redesigned the tooling layout to cut unnecessary movement between cycles and adjusted cooling channel placement to shorten cycle time. Applying this approach across three molds reduced average cycle time by twelve percent, which translated into faster turnaround for the client and lower per-unit cost for the company. That experience taught me that process efficiency isn't a matter of following a checklist of principles; it's about identifying where a system's constraints are hiding and redesigning around them.

Together, these two experiences have shown me that I'm drawn to problems where design decisions must be optimized against real-world constraints, whether those constraints are structural, as with the solar car, or operational, as with the molding tooling. That is why I'm applying to your program's design optimization track specifically, rather than a more general design curriculum: the tradeoff-driven work I've already done on the solar car and at Anderson Manufacturing is the kind of thinking your coursework in optimization methods and manufacturing-integrated design would let me formalize and extend. feedback2:
Thank you for sharing this draft. There's real substance here—you have two strong experiences to draw on, and the injection-molding statistic (twelve percent cycle time reduction) shows you can speak concretely about your impact. But right now the statement tells the reader what happened to you rather than showing who you are as an engineer and thinker, and the prose itself needs tightening. Let me walk through the main areas to work on, starting with the biggest structural issues and then moving to sentence-level concerns.

The opening line is the first thing to fix. "I have always been interested in mechanical engineering since I was young" is one of the most common openings in personal statements, and admissions readers see it constantly. It also doesn't do any real work—it doesn't tell us anything specific about you. Consider opening with a concrete moment, image, or problem instead: a specific challenge on the solar car, a moment of realization during the internship, or a question about design that has stuck with you. A vivid, specific opening will distinguish your statement immediately.

Related to this, the statement suffers from redundancy at both the sentence and paragraph level. In the first paragraph, you tell us three times, in slightly different words, that the solar car project sparked and confirmed your interest in mechanical engineering ("My interest in mechanical engineering comes from...", "Working on the solar car project was where I learned...", "The experience... showed me that mechanical engineering is a field where I can make a meaningful contribution"). Each of these sentences is making essentially the same claim without adding new information. The same pattern happens in the second paragraph with Anderson Manufacturing ("has made me certain that mechanical engineering is what I want to do"). Look for these repeated affirmations and cut most of them, letting the specific details of your work carry the emotional weight instead of restating your enthusiasm outright.

This connects to a "show, don't tell" issue that runs through the whole piece. You often name a skill or lesson in the abstract—"taught me a lot about how to apply theoretical knowledge to practical problems," "requires both technical skills and the ability to work with other people," "help me develop more advanced skills in design optimization and process efficiency"—without giving the reader the concrete detail that would make these claims convincing. What theoretical knowledge, applied to what practical problem, with what result? What did a design review meeting actually look like, and what tension between weight and structural integrity did you personally have to resolve, and how? The injection molding paragraph does this better because it gives a number, but even there you could say more about what you actually decided or changed, not just that you "applied lean manufacturing principles." Specificity is what turns a resume-in-prose into a personal statement.

Structurally, the essay reads as a list of tasks and generic takeaways rather than a narrative with development. Right now paragraph one is solar car, paragraph two is internship, and then the piece just stops after a brief line about the program. There's no conclusion that pulls the two experiences together, articulates your research or career goals, or explains what kind of engineer you want to become. Graduate admissions committees are looking for evidence of intellectual direction—what specific problems do you want to work on next, and why does graduate study (rather than industry, or a different program) get you there? You gesture at "design optimization and process efficiency" but don't say what that means for you concretely: a subfield, a type of research, a faculty member's work you admire. The closing sentence about the program's reputation and the design optimization track is thin—almost any applicant to almost any program could write that sentence. Strengthen it by naming specific faculty, labs, courses, or research questions at this program and connecting them explicitly to the interests you've just demonstrated through your experiences.

At the sentence level, there is a lot of repetitive structure that makes the prose monotonous: many sentences begin with "I worked on..." or "Working on..." or "The experience..." Reading it aloud, you'll notice the rhythm becomes flat and mechanical (no pun intended). Vary your sentence openings and lengths, and combine closely related ideas—for instance, "I worked on the suspension system and I worked on optimizing the aerodynamics of the vehicle frame" should simply be "I worked on the suspension system and on optimizing the vehicle's aerodynamics," or better, integrated into a sentence that also tells us what you learned from doing both.

There are also a few grammar and usage issues worth correcting. "I worked with a team of five other students where we meet weekly" has a tense inconsistency (meet should be met, since this is describing a completed experience) and misuses "where" to refer to a team of people rather than a place; you'd want something like "with whom I met weekly" or a restructured sentence. Referring to "the solar car project" and "Anderson Manufacturing" repeatedly by their full names, rather than using pronouns or shorter references after the first mention, makes the prose feel stiff; once you've named them, you can refer to "the project" or "the internship" or simply "there."

Finally, watch your word choice for vague, inflated phrases that could apply to almost any applicant: "meaningful contribution," "advanced skills," "passionate about," "strong reputation." These phrases aren't wrong, but they're generic filler that every reader has seen hundreds of times. Wherever you find one, ask whether you can replace it with something specific to your actual experience—a particular design decision, a specific course or research area at the target program, a precise career goal.

In short, you have good raw material: a hands-on team engineering project and a results-oriented internship. The next draft should cut the redundant statements of enthusiasm, replace generic claims with concrete details and outcomes, vary your sentence structure, and add a real concluding section that connects your experiences to specific, well-researched reasons for choosing this particular graduate program and a clear sense of what you want to do with the degree afterward.

During the final week before qualifying for our solar car's cross-country race, I found a two-millimeter deflection in one of the suspension mounts that threatened to fail under load. I spent that night back in the CAD model, recalculating tolerances I had only recently learned to use, trying to find a way to stiffen the joint without adding the weight that would slow the car down. That tension—between making something strong enough and making it light enough—turned out to define most of my work on the project, and it is what first showed me what mechanical engineering actually involves.

The solar car project was a team-based initiative in which students design and build a solar-powered vehicle to compete in a cross-country race. I worked on the suspension system and on optimizing the aerodynamics of the vehicle frame, which meant constantly weighing structural margins against drag and mass. Resolving the suspension problem, for instance, required switching to a thinner-walled tube with an internal rib rather than simply thickening the material, a change that added strength with minimal weight penalty. I also learned CAD software from scratch to model these changes, and I worked with a team of five other students with whom I met weekly to review designs and argue over tradeoffs. Those meetings taught me as much as the engineering itself: a good design decision had to survive being challenged by four other people before it was worth building.

I later spent two summers as an intern at Anderson Manufacturing, where I worked on injection molding processes and the optimization of tooling designs. I learned lean manufacturing principles through internal training and manuals, then applied them directly to three production molds—for example, by resequencing the cooling cycle and adjusting gate placement to cut redundant dwell time—reducing average cycle time by twelve percent across the three. That work made concrete something the solar car project had only suggested: that small, well-reasoned changes to a design or process can produce measurable gains at scale.

Together, these experiences have pointed me toward graduate study in design optimization, particularly the use of computational tools like topology optimization to resolve the same weight-versus-strength tradeoffs I encountered firsthand on the solar car's suspension. I am applying to your program because of Professor [Name]'s work on optimization algorithms for manufacturing constraints in the [Lab Name], which speaks directly to the kind of problem I ran into at Anderson Manufacturing: knowing a design can be improved but lacking a systematic way to search for the improvement. I am also drawn to your program's coursework in advanced manufacturing systems, which would let me build on the lean principles I applied as an intern with a more rigorous, quantitative foundation. My goal is to work on research that connects computational design tools directly to manufacturability, so that the kind of tradeoffs I resolved by trial and error in a machine shop can instead be resolved systematically, before a part is ever built.

# Feedback on Your Graduate School Personal Statement

Your personal statement has a strong foundation. You tell a coherent story that traces your intellectual development from a formative classroom experience through meaningful work experience to clear graduate aspirations. The narrative arc is sound, and you've done the important work of connecting your past experiences to your future goals and explaining why this particular program matters to you. These are the elements admissions committees want to see, and you've got them.

However, there are several issues that need attention before this is ready to submit, ranging from grammar to more subtle matters of voice and specificity.

Let's start with the most obvious problems. In the first paragraph, you write "I thought manufacturing would of been the most unstable." This is a common error: the phrase should be "would have been," not "would of." Similarly, in your second paragraph, you use "effect" when you mean "affect"—you're asking how policy interventions influence (affect) employment outcomes, not what effect they have on them. Wait, actually, I need to reconsider: you could use "effect" as a verb meaning to bring about change, but in context, "affect" (influence) is what you intend. These are the kind of errors that stand out sharply to admissions readers, so catching them is crucial.

Beyond grammar, there's a vocabulary issue in your second paragraph. You write that you're "particularly interested in how policy interventions effect employment outcomes," but you've already used the word "effect" earlier in the sentence structure. More importantly, "effect employment outcomes" is imprecise. Do you mean how interventions change, improve, influence, or shape employment outcomes? Be more specific about the relationship you're investigating.

The larger structural issue is that your statement could be more selective and focused. Right now, it covers a lot of ground—the introductory course, the specific dataset you built, the research conference presentation, your general interest in economics, your interest in graduate study, your interest in causal inference, your interest in applied microeconomics, your interest in labor economics, your interest in policy interventions, and your interest in economic inequality. That's a lot of interests compressed into a relatively short space. Graduate personal statements work best when they drill down into a few things deeply rather than listing many things broadly. Consider whether every single element serves your core narrative, or whether some could be trimmed to make room for greater depth.

For instance, the detail about manufacturing being unexpected is interesting and shows genuine engagement with your findings, but it takes up valuable space. The presentation at the undergraduate research conference is nice, but it's somewhat generic as an achievement. Ask yourself: what is the single most important thing an admissions committee needs to understand about you? Right now, the answer seems to be "I did data work, found it interesting, and want to do more in graduate school," but you could deepen this considerably.

Consider also the language you use to describe your journey. You write that "the work was tedious but meaningful," which is honest but somewhat deflating—you're kind of apologizing for the work rather than celebrating what you learned from it. When you describe being "nervous but did it anyway" about the presentation, that's relatable but also a bit self-diminishing. These constructions frame your experiences as things you endured rather than things you genuinely engaged with. Your writing will be stronger if you convey more confidence in the value of what you've done and learned.

There's also an opportunity to make your disciplinary understanding more sophisticated. You write that "Economics is the study of human behavior and decision-making," which is technically true but fairly elementary. This feels like a statement you might make in an introductory economics class, not in a graduate school application. For graduate study, admissions committees want to see that you understand economics at a deeper level. What specifically about how people make decisions under constraints fascinates you? How does your experience with wage data illuminate these broader questions?

Finally, the last paragraph does good work by connecting your interests to the specific program, but it could be more precise. You mention the program's emphasis on microeconomic theory and note specific faculty interests in minimum wage policy and job displacement. This is excellent—it shows you've done your homework. But you don't explain why those particular research areas matter to you beyond noting they exist. How does the faculty's work on minimum wage policy connect to your own emerging research questions? What specific questions would you want to explore in conversation with them? The more specific and thoughtful this connection, the more compelling your statement becomes.

In sum, focus on correcting the grammatical errors immediately, trim some of the broader list of interests to create space for greater depth, strengthen the language around your experiences to convey genuine enthusiasm rather than endurance, demonstrate more sophisticated disciplinary thinking, and deepen your explanation of why this program specifically aligns with your goals. These revisions will significantly strengthen what is already a competent draft.

After weeks of cleaning data, handling missing values, and running regressions, I found that leisure and hospitality experienced the greatest wage volatility—not manufacturing, which I had expected to be least stable. That result made me reconsider what I thought I knew about labor markets. Manufacturing wages are often shaped by long-term contracts and unionization, while leisure and hospitality workers are exposed more directly to short-run shifts in consumer demand and staffing needs. The finding didn't just surprise me; it made me want to know why. That question is what pulled me from simply describing patterns in data toward wanting to explain them.

This kind of question first took shape during Introduction to Econometrics with Professor Maria Hernandez, where we used the Current Population Survey to study labor market trends and I first became interested in wage inequality. The internship gave me a chance to pursue that interest with real data. Professor Hernandez later invited me to present the wage volatility findings at the university's undergraduate research conference, an experience that showed me how much I enjoy defending an empirical claim in front of people who will push back on it.

That distinction—between documenting that volatility exists and identifying what causes it—is exactly what I want to pursue in graduate study. My internship showed me that I enjoy working with messy, real-world data, but it also showed me the limits of what descriptive analysis alone can tell me. I want to deepen my technical skills in causal inference and applied microeconomics so that I can move beyond correlations like the one I found in the wage data and ask, for example, whether it is demand volatility, weaker labor protections, or some other mechanism driving instability in low-wage sectors. Graduate school would let me pursue research in labor economics more rigorously. I am particularly interested in how policy interventions affect employment outcomes for low-wage workers.

My long-term goal is to work in policy or research where I can contribute analysis that helps address economic inequality. Your program's emphasis on microeconomic theory, combined with your faculty's work on minimum wage policy and job displacement, would let me build the causal inference toolkit I need to take the wage volatility puzzle further—to test which mechanisms actually explain why some low-wage sectors are so much more exposed to instability than others, and to turn that analysis into evidence that can inform policy.

# Feedback on Your Graduate School Personal Statement

Your personal statement has genuine strengths that will resonate with admissions committees. You tell a coherent story about discovering your passion for econometrics through a meaningful class experience, then demonstrating that passion through internship work. The narrative arc from curiosity to concrete research to future goals is clear and purposeful. You also do something important by connecting your technical interests to a larger social concern—addressing economic inequality—which shows the "why" behind your work, not just the "what." This matters in graduate applications.

Now let's address some issues that are preventing this from reaching its full potential.

**Grammar and mechanics:** You have a few errors that will undermine your credibility in an academic application. In the first paragraph, you write "would of been" when you mean "would have been." This is a common mistake, but it's especially noticeable in formal writing where precision is expected. In the second paragraph, you write "effect employment outcomes" when you need "affect"—effect is a noun, affect is the verb you need here. These errors suggest you haven't proofread carefully, and in a personal statement where every word counts, that matters. Read your work aloud before submitting it; these mistakes are much easier to catch when you hear them.

**Vocabulary and word choice:** You have some vague moments that weaken your voice. When you describe the internship work as "tedious but meaningful," you're reaching for an easy contrast without really explaining what made it meaningful. What specifically about cleaning data and running regressions mattered to you? Similarly, you say you were "nervous but did it anyway" when presenting your research—but why mention the nervousness at all if you're not going to explore it? A brief acknowledgment of having overcome something can be effective, but only if you make clear why it mattered. The phrase "I realize now" in your second paragraph is also somewhat soft; it suggests a retrospective realization, but admissions committees want to see conviction, not passive reflection.

**Internal paragraph construction:** Your first paragraph does a lot of work. It establishes the source of your interest, shows you took initiative as an intern, describes concrete research outcomes, and includes a personal anecdote about presenting. That's actually too much. The presentation story, while nice, doesn't add substantive information about your skills or interests—it mostly shows that Professor Hernandez noticed your work, which is more about her validation than about what you learned. Consider whether this detail is earning its place, or whether you could use that space to go deeper into what surprised you about your findings or what the wage volatility data made you curious about.

**Specificity and detail:** You mention an "unexpected" finding about leisure and hospitality, which is good—it shows you were thinking critically. But you don't explain *why* this was unexpected or what you learned from this surprise. Did it change how you think about sectoral vulnerability? Did it prompt follow-up questions? Graduate programs want to see that you don't just run analyses; you think about what they mean. Similarly, in your second paragraph, you mention the program's work on minimum wage policy and job displacement, which shows research, but you haven't explained how your interests align with those topics in specific ways.

**Achieving your purpose:** The fundamental purpose of a personal statement is to help admissions committees understand who you are as a potential researcher and colleague, and to convince them you'll thrive in their program. You've established interest and some relevant experience, which is good. But you haven't fully conveyed your intellectual maturity or your capacity for independent thinking. The best personal statements show the reader how your mind works—what kinds of questions you ask, how you approach problems, what you find genuinely puzzling about your field. Right now, your statement tells admissions officers that you discovered econometrics, did an internship, and want to continue in the field. That's solid, but it doesn't quite distinguish you from other strong candidates with similar trajectories.

**Overall suggestions:** Consider deepening one or two moments rather than covering so much ground. For instance, you could expand on what you learned from the unexpected findings about wage volatility—what follow-up questions did it raise? Or you could explore in more detail why the intersection of labor economics and policy specifically appeals to you beyond "helping address inequality." This second approach might mean cutting something else (perhaps the presentation anecdote) to create space for genuine intellectual reflection.

Proofread meticulously for grammar. Make sure every sentence in the statement does essential work—establishing your background, showing your thinking, or explaining why this program is the right next step. Read the program's website carefully and mention specific faculty or research areas by name, so the admissions committee sees you're genuinely interested in their work, not just using a template statement.

You have the foundation of a good statement here. With revision focused on depth, specificity, and proofreading, it can be strong.

This is a solid foundation with genuine substance—you have a real research narrative, specific technical detail, and an identifiable trajectory from coursework to internship to research goals. That's more than many applicants bring. But the passage needs tightening and sharpening in several areas before it will do its job effectively.

The most important issue is that your two paragraphs are doing overlapping work and the piece as a whole lacks a clear argumentative arc. Right now the structure is roughly chronological (class, then internship, then conference, then "now I realize...") but personal statements are most persuasive when they're organized around a claim rather than a timeline. Consider what single impression you want the admissions committee to walk away with—something like "I have already done the work of a junior researcher in labor economics and I know precisely what I want to study next"—and then organize every sentence to build toward that. As it stands, the transition between paragraphs ("I realize now that I want to deepen my technical skills...") feels like a reset rather than a natural culmination, which makes the essay feel like two separate drafts stitched together rather than one continuous argument.

Related to this, the first paragraph tries to do too much and consequently rushes several moments that deserve more weight. The sentence about being nervous but presenting anyway is a good instinct—admissions committees like to see resilience—but it's mentioned so briefly it doesn't land. Either develop it (what did presenting teach you? did questions from the audience shape your thinking?) or cut it. Similarly, the line "Economics is the study of human behavior and decision-making" is a textbook-style generality that doesn't tell the reader anything about you specifically; sentences like this are common in weaker personal statements because they sound authoritative but are actually filler. Cut it or replace it with a sentence that connects specifically to what you found compelling in your own data.

On the topic of specificity, you're strongest when you're concrete—CPS data, 2015–2021 wage tracking, leisure and hospitality volatility—and weakest when you generalize. Push further in the concrete direction. For instance, "there are interesting questions you can answer when you know how to handle messy data properly" is vague; tell us what question, specifically, intrigued you. Did the wage volatility finding raise a hypothesis you couldn't test with the data you had? That unanswered question is exactly the kind of thing that should motivate your interest in graduate training, and naming it would make the link between your internship and your future research agenda much tighter and more convincing.

Your final paragraph, where you name the program's strengths and faculty, is important and you're right to include it, but it currently reads as a list rather than a fit argument. Naming that your target professors work on minimum wage policy and job displacement is good, but you should draw an explicit line between their work and your own question or method—for example, if your wage volatility finding relates to job displacement research, say so directly. Fit paragraphs are more convincing when they show you've thought about how your specific project would extend or engage with specific faculty work, rather than simply listing subject-matter overlap.

On mechanics: "would of been" should be "would have been"—this is a common speech-to-writing error but it's the kind of thing that stands out negatively in a formal application, so proofread carefully for it and similar issues. "Effect employment outcomes" should be "affect employment outcomes"; affect is the verb (to influence), effect is usually the noun (a result). These are small errors but personal statements are judged partly on your care and precision as a writer, especially for a field like economics that values precision, so it's worth reading the piece aloud slowly or having someone else proofread it.

A few sentences also suffer from wordiness or awkward construction. By contrast, "I realize now that I want to deepen my technical skills in causal inference and applied microeconomics through graduate study" is a bit clunky and abstract for an opening sentence of the second paragraph; consider leading with something more vivid, perhaps a specific unresolved question from your internship, and then pivoting to the graduate skills you'd need to answer it.

Finally, consider the ending. The essay currently closes on programmatic fit, which is appropriate, but you might strengthen the close by circling back to the personal motivation you opened with—inequality, the specific finding that surprised you, or the moment of presenting your research—so the essay feels unified rather than ending on a purely institutional note. The main work now is condensing redundant or generic sentences, deepening the two or three moments that matter most (the surprising finding, the conference presentation, the connection to your target faculty), and making sure every paragraph explicitly serves the central claim about who you are as an emerging researcher and why this particular program is the next right step.

My interest in environmental science began when I volunteered at the Chesapeake Bay Foundation during my junior year, where I learned about the dead zone expansion and nitrogen runoff from agricultural sources. This experience made me realize how interconnected human activities and ecosystem health truly are, and since then, I have been committed to understanding and solving these problems through science. In my undergraduate thesis, I examined how different cover crop species—specifically rye, clover, and vetch—affect soil microbial communities in the Shenandoah Valley region of Virginia; this research was conducted over two growing seasons and involved collecting soil samples from fifteen different farms. The results showed that legume cover crops, particularly clover, promoted nitrogen fixation and increased microbial diversity compared to non-legume crops, which were important findings for farmers trying to reduce synthetic fertilizer use. This field is what I am passionate about, and I believe that graduate study will allow me to deepen my knowledge and contribute meaningful research to address challenges like water quality degradation and agricultural sustainability. Beyond my research experience, I have also worked as a teaching assistant for Environmental Biology, where I helped students understand how agricultural runoff, watershed management, and soil conservation practices connect human land use to downstream ecosystem health. Throughout these experiences, I developed strong laboratory and field skills, including proficiency with DNA sequencing, soil analysis, and statistical modeling using R; equally important, I cultivated a deep respect for the importance of bridging the gap between scientific findings and practical agricultural solutions.

My time at the Chesapeake Bay Foundation and my cover crop research have solidified my desire to pursue a career in applied soil science, particularly focusing on sustainable agriculture and soil health. This work gave me exposure to real-world agricultural challenges and the diverse perspectives of farmers who are often skeptical of new practices. I am drawn to your program specifically because of Dr. Patricia Chen's research on soil carbon sequestration in conservation agriculture systems. I am eager to explore whether the microbial shifts I observed under different cover crop regimes correspond to measurable changes in soil carbon storage, and I hope to investigate how conservation practices might be scaled across diverse farm sizes without imposing significant costs on producers. Your program's emphasis on both rigorous research methodology and community engagement aligns closely with these goals, and I am especially interested in combining lab-based soil analysis with the kind of farmer outreach that made my undergraduate research meaningful. My goal is to develop innovative soil management practices that farmers can adopt without significant economic investment, thereby improving outcomes for the land while supporting rural livelihoods. This work requires not just technical expertise but also the ability to communicate across different communities, and I am committed to bringing both to my graduate studies.

# Personal Statement – Environmental Science Graduate Program

My interest in environmental science began when I volunteered at the Chesapeake Bay Foundation during my junior year, where I learned about the dead zone expansion and nitrogen runoff from agricultural sources. That experience made clear how interconnected human activities and ecosystem health truly are, and it set the course I have followed since: I want to spend my career using science to solve environmental problems, and I believe graduate study is the next step toward that goal.

In my undergraduate thesis, I examined how different cover crop species—rye, clover, and vetch—affect soil microbial communities in the Shenandoah Valley region of Virginia. The research spanned two growing seasons and involved collecting soil samples from fifteen different farms. The results showed that legume cover crops, particularly clover, promoted nitrogen fixation and increased microbial diversity compared to non-legume crops. For farmers trying to reduce synthetic fertilizer use, that distinction matters: clover-based rotations could cut fertilizer inputs while maintaining soil health.

Beyond this research, I worked as a teaching assistant for Environmental Biology, where I helped students understand the complexities of ecology and the ways human and natural systems intersect. Explaining nitrogen cycling and soil ecology to undergraduates taught me to translate technical findings into language non-specialists could use—a skill I later relied on when discussing results with the farmers whose land I sampled. Through these experiences, I developed strong laboratory and field skills, including proficiency with DNA sequencing, soil analysis, and statistical modeling in R, along with a commitment to connecting scientific findings to practical agricultural solutions.

These experiences—the volunteering, the fifteen-farm study, and the teaching—have solidified my desire to pursue applied environmental science, particularly sustainable agriculture and soil health. Working across fifteen farms in the Shenandoah Valley exposed me to farmers who are often skeptical of new practices, and it taught me that good soil science means little without buy-in from the people who work the land.

I am drawn to your program because of Dr. Patricia Chen's research on soil carbon sequestration in conservation agriculture systems. My cover crop data showed that clover increased microbial diversity; I want to test whether that same diversity gain corresponds to measurable increases in soil organic carbon, extending Dr. Chen's carbon sequestration models to legume-based cover crop systems rather than the tillage systems she has studied to date. Your program's emphasis on both rigorous methodology and community engagement matches that goal.

My aim is to develop soil management practices that farmers can adopt using inputs they already have—rotating in legume cover crops rather than purchasing new equipment or synthetic fertilizer—so that environmental gains do not come at the farmer's expense. Reaching that goal will require the same two skills I have been building since my time at the Chesapeake Bay Foundation: rigorous lab work, and the ability to explain that work to the people who will use it. My teaching experience taught me the second skill as much as my research taught me the first, and I intend to bring both to Dr. Chen's lab and to your program.

The most immediate problem is grammar, and it appears in enough places that it will distract readers from your substance. Several sentences have subject-verb agreement errors: "how different cover crop species... affects soil microbial communities" should be "affect," since "species" here is plural in this context; similarly, "Environmental science are what I am passionate about" needs "is," and "the ways in which human and natural systems intersects" needs "intersect." You also have a comma splice in "In my undergraduate thesis, I examined... this research was conducted over two growing seasons," where two independent clauses are joined only by a comma—this needs a period, semicolon, or conjunction. Later, "The results showed that legume cover crops, particularly clover, promoting nitrogen fixation" should be "promoted," and "The work I done at fifteen different farms" should be "The work I did" or "have done." These aren't minor slips—application readers often treat grammatical precision as a proxy for scientific rigor, so it's worth proofreading line by line, ideally reading the piece aloud to catch these agreement and tense issues.

Beyond grammar, the sentences themselves are frequently overloaded. Many run past 40-50 words, stacking multiple clauses with commas rather than breaking ideas into digestible units. For instance, the opening sentence packs in the volunteer experience, the dead zone problem, the runoff issue, and your realization about interconnection all in one breath. Consider splitting these into two or three sentences so each idea lands with its own weight. This will also help you vary your rhythm—right now nearly every sentence follows a similar long, clause-heavy pattern, which becomes monotonous.

The first paragraph tries to do too much: it introduces your origin story, describes your thesis research in detail, makes a broad statement of passion, mentions your TA work, and lists your technical skills. This makes it hard for a reader to follow a throughline. I'd recommend dedicating one paragraph to your foundational motivation (the Chesapeake Bay experience) and clearly transitioning into your research as the natural continuation of that interest, rather than presenting the passion statement ("Environmental science are what I am passionate about") in the middle, which reads as a generic aside rather than an organizing thesis. The TA experience and skills list feel bolted on at the end of paragraph one; they might work better integrated into a dedicated "skills and teaching" section, or trimmed if they're not central to your argument.

You also repeat material across the two paragraphs—both mention the Chesapeake Bay Foundation and the fifteen farms in the Shenandoah Valley almost verbatim. Since the second paragraph reintroduces experiences already described in the first, it reads more like a restart than a continuation. Consider using the second paragraph exclusively to pivot forward: briefly reference your past work in a single clause, then spend most of the space on why this specific program and Dr. Chen's research meet your goals, and what you intend to contribute or investigate in the program itself.

In terms of content and purpose, the passage does a good job naming specific, credible details—crop types, sample sizes, growing seasons, R programming, DNA sequencing—which lends authenticity. However, the statement would be stronger if you connected these details more explicitly to a forward-looking research question or intellectual problem you want to pursue in graduate school, rather than just cataloguing past accomplishments. Right now, the goals paragraph is strong on programmatic fit (naming Dr. Chen, noting the emphasis on methodology and community engagement) but relatively generic on what you specifically want to study or discover. Sharpening this—perhaps by naming a specific question about soil carbon sequestration you'd want to explore with Dr. Chen, or describing what "innovative soil management practices" might look like—would make your fit argument more concrete and less like a checklist.

Finally, some word choices could be elevated. Phrases like "Environmental science are what I am passionate about" and "committed to understanding and solving environmental problems through science" are somewhat generic and would benefit from more specific, active language showing rather than telling your commitment. You use "committed" twice and lean heavily on abstract nouns (interconnection, complexities, perspectives) where more concrete verbs and images would carry more persuasive weight. Also watch your sentence openers—many sentences begin with "I," which becomes repetitive; varying your syntax (leading with a dependent clause, a specific detail, or an active verb) will make the prose feel more dynamic.

In sum, prioritize fixing the grammatical agreement errors and run-on sentences first, since these affect credibility immediately. Then work on tightening structure so each paragraph has a clear, non-overlapping purpose, and finally sharpen your forward-looking research goals so the "fit" argument feels as specific and well-evidenced as your description of past work.

This research was conducted over two growing seasons and involved collecting soil samples from fifteen different farms. The results showed that legume cover crops, particularly clover, promoted nitrogen fixation and increased microbial diversity compared to non-legume crops. These findings suggest that farmers could reduce their reliance on synthetic nitrogen fertilizer by incorporating clover into rotational planting, lowering input costs while maintaining soil fertility.

Beyond my research experience, I have also worked as a teaching assistant for Environmental Biology, where I helped students understand the complexities of ecology and the ways in which human and natural systems intersect. Through these experiences, I developed strong laboratory and field skills, including proficiency with DNA sequencing, soil analysis, and statistical modeling using R. Just as importantly, I gained a deep respect for the work of bridging scientific findings and practical agricultural solutions. Environmental science is what I am passionate about, and I believe graduate study will allow me to deepen my knowledge and contribute meaningful research to challenges like water quality degradation and agricultural sustainability.

# Feedback on Your Personal Statement

Your personal statement tells a coherent story about discovering computer science and developing focused research interests, which is a strong foundation for a graduate application. However, there are several issues—ranging from grammar to voice—that undermine the impact of what you're trying to communicate. I'll address the most important problems first.

**Grammar and Subject-Verb Agreement**

You have multiple verb tense and agreement errors that distract from your content and suggest carelessness in revision. In your first sentence, you write "I take CS 201" when it should be "I took CS 201," since you're describing a past event. Later, you write "My goals for graduate school is" when "goals" is plural and requires "are." You also write "I believes" instead of "I believe," and "the work I done" instead of "the work I did." Additionally, "your faculty" should be "your faculty members" or simply "the faculty," and "a systems that is" should be "systems that are." These errors appear frequently enough that they create a cumulative effect. Before submitting any application materials, you should read your statement aloud slowly and carefully, or better yet, have someone else proofread it. Graduate admissions committees expect polished writing, and errors like these may undermine their confidence in your attention to detail.

**Pronoun Case**

In the first paragraph, you write "me and five other students competed," but the correct form is "five other students and I competed." This is a common mistake, but it's one that admissions committees notice. You can avoid the error by reversing the order: "five other students and I" always sounds right, whereas "me and five other students" does not.

**Voice and Authenticity**

Beyond mechanics, your statement feels somewhat generic in places. Phrases like "I am excited about the opportunity to study at your institution" and "I am particularly drawn to the work of your faculty in these areas" don't tell the reader anything specific about you or your genuine interest. These sentences could apply to almost any candidate at almost any program. Instead, consider what specifically excites you about this program. Why is Professor Martinez's work compelling to you? What particular challenge in database systems or distributed computing has captured your imagination? The strongest moment in your statement is when you describe optimizing database queries at TechCorp and seeing theory apply to real problems—that's concrete and personal. You should deepen that kind of specificity throughout.

**Organization and Narrative Flow**

Your two paragraphs are somewhat awkwardly divided. The first paragraph mixes your initial career decision, an internship, and a competition, while the second jumps to your goals and then circles back to justify them through past experience. Consider reorganizing so that you move more logically from discovery to experience to future direction. You might also trim some details: do admissions committees need to know that you got an A in CS 201, or that you placed second rather than first in the competition? These details don't strengthen your argument and can make the statement feel padded. Focus on what genuinely shaped your thinking.

**Word Choice and Tone**

A few word choices could be more precise or sophisticated. You write that something "was exciting" and that an achievement "was really good"—these are conversational phrases that weaken your statement. Instead of "exciting" or "really good," try to characterize the experience more specifically. What made it valuable? What did it reveal to you? Similarly, "helped me to improve" is slightly awkward; "helped me improve" is more direct. These small refinements matter in academic writing.

**Addressing Your Purpose**

Graduate admissions committees want to understand why you're applying now, why you're applying to their program in particular, and what you'll contribute. Your statement does address why you're drawn to computer science and what research areas interest you, which is good. However, you need to strengthen the section explaining why their program specifically is the right fit. Mentioning Professor Martinez and their lab is helpful, but you could go further. What questions do you hope to answer in graduate school? What research problems excite you? The more specific you are about your intellectual interests and goals, the more persuasive your application becomes.

Start by carefully correcting all grammar and agreement errors. Then, rewrite the statement to deepen its specificity and remove generic phrases. Trim unnecessary details and reorganize so the narrative flows more naturally from past to future. Finally, have someone else read it aloud to you—your ear will catch awkwardness that your eye might miss.
